Shareable abstract Childhood interstitial lung disease (chILD) diagnosis requires multiple tests, often delaying targeted treatments. Supportive care starts early, while specific therapies follow diagnosis. This review summarises current and emerging treatments. https://bit.ly/3M0dYD0 status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2025 Mar 26; Accepted 2026 Jan 15; Collection date 2026 Jan. Introduction Childhood interstitial lung disease (chILD) is a heterogeneous group of over 200 rare lung diseases [ 1 , 2 ], with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 100 000 children [ 3 , 4 ]. Recent epidemiological data from a multicentre Spanish study reported a chILD prevalence of 46.5 cases per million children and an incidence of 8.2 new cases per million per year, higher than previously described [ 5 ]. Moreover, A recent nationwide French study within the RespiRare network reported a chILD prevalence of 44 cases per million children and an incidence of 4.4 new cases per million per year, confirming higher rates than previously described [ 6 ]. Since chILD may affect different lung compartments, including the interstitium, airways, alveolar space and vascular bed, the term “diffuse lung disease” has been proposed [ 7 , 8 ]. Despite its rarity, paediatric pulmonologists must recognise these diseases for timely diagnosis and management [ 9 ]. The severity of chILD ranges from mild and nonspecific symptoms, with a possible late diagnosis, to a severe clinical presentation [ 10 – 13 ]. The clinical spectrum varies from early-onset neonatal respiratory distress (typically in a term baby), to later and nonspecific signs, such as hypoxia, tachy-dyspnoea, failure to thrive, dry cough, wheezing, pulmonary hypertension, digital clubbing and/or cyanosis [ 13 – 15 ]. The diagnostic criteria and the classification of chILD have been revised several times over the past decade. In 2013, chILD was defined as the presence of at least three of the following criteria: 1) respiratory symptoms, 2) clinical signs of respiratory insufficiency, 3) hypoxaemia or low pulse oxygen saturation, 4) diffuse parenchymal lung disease on chest radiography or thoracic computed tomography (CT) [ 16 ]. Then, B ush et al . [ 1 ], on behalf of the chILD European Union working groups (chILD-EU), proposed a diagnostic flowchart in which high-resolution chest CT was the cornerstone examination. Later, N athan et al . [ 13 , 17 , 18 ] provided a comprehensive, up-to-date review of the stepwise diagnostic process. They proposed a first step aimed at raising the suspicion of chILD (based on clinical evaluation, family history assessment, routine biological tests, chest radiography and echocardiography) and a second step, aimed at confirming and classifying interstitial lung disease (ILD), that requires specialised expertise and further investigations, including high-resolution CT (HRCT), bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), specific laboratory tests, pulmonary function tests, genetic tests and/or lung biopsy. Thus, a team-based multidisciplinary approach is essential to achieve a correct diagnosis, in which paediatric pulmonologist play the most relevant role [ 19 ]. Regarding the classification of chILD, a 2004 report by the European Respiratory Society (ERS) task force (TF) on chronic ILD in immunocompetent children proposed the first classification specifically designed for children, closely aligned with the adult classification [ 20 ]. In 2007, a mainly pathology-based classification for diffuse lung disease in children under 2 years was developed through a collaboration between pathologists and clinicians [ 7 ]. In 2015, a study gathered clinical and histological data from patients aged 2–18 years presenting with diffuse lung disease, categorising the condition [ 21 ]. Later, this classification was extended to all paediatric age groups [ 1 ]. In 2009 and 2015, this classification was adopted and expanded to encompass all cases of chILD, irrespective of the child's age and the availability of a histopathological diagnosis [ 22 , 23 ]. Then, in 2015, K itazawa and K ure [ 24 ] proposed an aetiological classification system. Recently, G riese et al . [ 25 ] suggested an aetiologic and age-overarching classification of diffuse lung diseases with four main categories, 1) lung-only (native parenchymal) disorders, 2) systemic disease-related disorders, 3) exposure-related disorders, and 4) vascular disorders. The diagnostic workup of suspected chILD requires a structured, stepwise and multidisciplinary approach [ 26 ]. Initial evaluation should include a detailed medical and family history, thorough physical examination, assessment of hypoxaemia and high-resolution chest imaging, which together form the cornerstone of diagnosis [ 26 ]. Additional investigations, such as pulmonary function testing, specific laboratory assessments, bronchoscopy with BAL, echocardiography, genetic testing and lung biopsy, are selected based on the individual clinical presentation and available resources. Bronchoscopy allows assessment of airway anatomy and the collection of BAL and/or bronchial biopsy specimens. Although only a limited number of diagnoses can be directly confirmed through specific cytological staining, bronchoscopy with BAL is used to exclude other causes of respiratory symptoms, such as lower respiratory tract infections or anatomical abnormalities [ 27 , 28 ]. Moreover, lung biopsy represents the final step in the diagnostic work-up of children with suspected chILD and, in some cases, it remains the only procedure that enables a definitive etiological diagnosis [ 29 ]. In this context, transbronchial lung cryobiopsy is emerging as a less invasive alternative to surgical lung biopsy, showing a high diagnostic yield while potentially reducing procedural morbidity, although current evidence is limited by small sample sizes, nonstandardised techniques and the lack of comparative trials [ 30 ]. Over recent years, advances in molecular genetics have significantly enhanced the diagnostic process, allowing the identification of pathogenic variants and, in many cases, reducing the need for invasive procedures such as lung biopsy [ 26 ]. However, even in genetically defined diseases, lung biopsy may still provide clinically relevant information that influences treatment decisions; for example, in children with chILD, histological confirmation of clinically significant fibrosis may be valuable when considering antifibrotic therapy [ 9 , 31 ]. As for treatment, supportive measures are initiated and then followed, if possible, by more targeted therapies once the disease is identified. This systematic review aims to 1) describe the current knowledge regarding different treatment strategies for chILD related to primary parenchymal disorder and 2) critically appraise, compare and qualitatively summarise the current evidence on old and emerging therapies for chILD. Material and methods This review was carried out according to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. It has been registered in PROSPERO with ID 1020225. A literature search was performed in Medline and Scopus to identify articles published from June 2000 to March 2024 using a combination of keywords and medical subject headings (MeSH), including “childhood interstitial lung disease”, “diffuse interstitial lung disease”, “treatment” and “therapy”. Boolean operators (AND, OR) were utilised to refine the search. To account for the rapid evolution of the field, major and highly relevant publications published after the end of the systematic search (March 2024) were also considered and incorporated where appropriate. All records were pooled and de-duplicated. Two independent reviewers (V. Tonazzo and R.J. Castaldo) screened for eligibility firstly titles and abstracts, and then full-text articles. Full-text articles of potentially relevant studies were retrieved and assessed for inclusion. Any disagreements between these two authors were resolved by a third author (V.A. Ferraro). Covidence systematic review software (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) was used, allowing the three reviewers to navigate the steps of this systematic review more efficiently. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: Population: children (aged 0–18 years) diagnosed with ILD classified as those more prevalent in childhood related to primary parenchymal lung disorders. Intervention: any pharmacological or nonpharmacological treatment. Study design: randomised controlled trials (RCTs), clinical trials, case reports, meta-analyses, reviews and systematic reviews. Language: English. Data were extracted using a standardised form, including the following information: Study characteristics (author, year, country, design). Participant demographics (age, sex, diagnosis). Treatment modalities (pharmacological agents, nonpharmacological interventions). Outcomes measured. Adverse effects reported. Conditions in which ILD occurs as part of systemic immune dysregulation disorders, as well as ILD related to environmental or exposure-related insults or vascular diseases, were excluded. As this review involved analysis of previously published studies, no ethical approval was required. Results Of the 5775 publications returned from the initial search, 100 studies met the inclusion criteria. The remaining papers were excluded due to duplicate datasets (n=1929), lack of relevant data (n=3698), outdated publications (n=10), non-English language (n=23) and inability to obtain the original article (n=15) ( figure 1 ). Among the 100 studies included in our systematic review, 51 (50%) were reviews or TF reports from several scientific societies, 40 (41%) case reports or case series, five (5%) RCTs and four (4%) preclinical studies on emerging therapies. FIGURE 1 PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) flow diagram used to outline the study selection process. As for RCTs and case reports or series, the majority of articles originate from high-income countries (n=40/45, 89%), reflecting better access to resources and advanced diagnostic techniques. Studies from low-middle and upper-middle income countries represent a smaller proportion (n=5/45, 11%). The most frequently reported countries were the United States and France, but the great majority of articles were multinational studies. Regarding the age of patients analysed in clinical case reports, most of the articles described neonates or infants under 2 years of age (n=30/40, 75%), while others considered patients aged 0–18 years (n=10/40, 25%). In order to provide a clearer description of the data analysed, we divided the presentation of the studies into two parts. First, we describe available chILD therapeutic options in general, organised by treatment type. Subsequently, we report treatments categorised by specific pathology. Exploring therapeutic options for chILD Therapy for chILD remained unstandardised for many years due to their rarity and the wide range of underlying conditions. In recent years, several collaborative networks have been established to advance research on chILD, including the US chILD Research Network (chILDRN) and chILD Foundation, as well as European (CRC chILDEU, RespiRare) and Australasian (chILDRANZ) networks [ 32 , 33 ]. All these networks contribute to the expansion of basic and translational research focused on chILD diseases [ 34 ]. Overall, such collaborative networks and multidisciplinary team-based approaches contribute to the development of best practices and support the establishment of virtual centres of excellence for rare paediatric lung diseases. Management relies on case series, case reports, clinical experience and indirect evidence from adults’ pulmonary fibrosis (PF) or other chronic lung diseases. Most chILD treatments are empirical, aiming to suppress inflammatory processes in order to prevent PF. For the first time in 2004 [ 20 ] an ERS TF outlined the most common therapeutic options in chILD. Authors highlighted the lack of standardised management, with significant variability in dosage and duration of treatments across centres. Among the 172 children analysed, systemic corticosteroids (orally or intravenous) were the preferred treatment (80%) at diagnosis, followed by hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) (18%), alone or combined with corticosteroids. Other treatments (13%) included azathioprine, cyclophosphamide and methotrexate. With the growing recognition that chILD is an entity distinct from adult ILD, the first international practice guideline on chILD treatment was published in 2013 by the American Thoracic Society (ATS) [ 16 ]. Acknowledging the absence of RCTs, the guideline committee employed a systematic approach to collect, review and grade the available evidence. As for systemic corticosteroids or HCQ, the guidelines highlighted side-effects risks and the limited evidence supporting therapeutic benefits. Consequently, they recommended a cautious, case-by-case approach to the use of these treatments in chILD therapy. Moreover, the guidelines described the importance of supportive care for chILD and highlighted lung transplantation as a potential therapeutic option for infants with severe, life-threatening forms of chILD. In 2015 [ 1 ], 2 years later, European guidelines were released on behalf of the chILD-EU Collaboration. These recommended protocols were developed using the Delphi method, surveying over 100 clinicians worldwide to harmonise treatment approaches. The guidelines proposed specific pharmacological therapies with suggested dosages, distinguishing between paediatric ILD patients who were ventilated or at risk of requiring ventilation and those who were not ( table 1 ). TABLE 1 Most frequently used pharmacological therapies for children Methylprednisolone Prednisolone HCQ Azithromycin chILD not ventilated or close to ventilation Intravenous 10 mg·kg −1 or 500 mg·m −2 Oral 2 mg·kg −1 , as alternative to methylprednisolone pulses 6.5–10 mg·kg −1 10 mg·kg −1 3 days per week chILD ventilated or close to ventilation Intravenous 10 mg·kg −1 or 500 mg·m −2 Oral 1 mg·kg −1 , used in between pulses of methylprednisolone 6.5–10 mg·kg −1 10 mg·kg −1 3 days per week chILD: childhood interstitial lung disease; HCQ: hydroxychloroquine. Information from [ 1 ]. Common treatments for chILD include supportive care, corticosteroids, HCQ and azithromycin [ 19 , 35 ], while less used treatments are azathioprine, cyclophosphamide and colchicine. It is mandatory for paediatric pulmonologists to understand side-effects in order to implement effective monitoring strategies [ 36 ]. Below, we provide a summary of the latest evidence regarding therapeutic options for chILD, including emerging therapies from preclinical studies and recently published RCTs. Supportive treatments All patients with chILD should receive supportive care, as established by ATS guidelines in 2013 [ 16 ]. Oxygen therapy is essential and may be required during exercise, feeding or continuously [ 37 ], sometimes coupled with invasive or noninvasive ventilation and respiratory physiotherapy [ 16 ]. Monitoring growth and weight gain is crucial, ensuring adequate caloric intake and proper nutrition [ 38 ]. Optimising nutritional status can improve growth, lung function and overall outcomes, and should be approached in a stepwise manner, starting with preventive counselling and dietary modifications, followed by oral supplements or enteral feeding when necessary [ 39 ]. Avoiding harmful environmental exposures, such as tobacco smoke, is essential [ 40 ]. Children with ILD can benefit from immunisations, including the pneumococcal vaccine and annual influenza vaccination [ 41 ]. Respiratory syncytial virus immunoprophylaxis may be useful but its real effectiveness remains to be proved [ 42 ]. Additionally, comprehensive family-centred care is advised, including social and psychological support, education, and support from care providers, to improve the quality of life for both patients and their families [ 16 , 40 ]. Corticosteroids Corticosteroids have been the cornerstone of chILD treatment, potentially suppressing immune-mediated alveolitis and systemic inflammation, providing repair mechanisms, and preventing fibrosis progression [ 43 ]. Moreover, in surfactant protein (SP) C disorder, corticosteroids have been shown to reduce SP-C mRNA levels and promote the expression of a less stable protein isoform [ 44 ]. Since the ERS TF in 2004 [ 20 ], chILD treatment typically involves oral prednisolone (1–2 mg·kg −1 daily) or pulsed i. v . methylprednisolone (10–30 mg·kg −1 daily for 3 days, repeated monthly for 3–6 months), depending on individual clinical response. In 2015, the European guidelines [ 1 ] provided detailed initial therapeutic doses for both ventilated (or near to ventilation) and nonventilated children with chILD. For i.v. therapy, a dose of methylprednisolone of 10 mg·kg −1 or 500 mg·m −2 was recommended for both ventilated and nonventilated children, with the option to increase to 30 mg·kg −1 in severe cases. Ventilated patients were noted to have a shorter expected response time (7 days versus 28 days). Oral prednisone was recommended at the dose of 1 mg·kg −1 for use between pulses of methylprednisolone in ventilated patients or at 2 mg·kg −1 daily as an alternative to methylprednisolone pulses in nonventilated patients. Guidelines did not provide recommendations on the duration of corticosteroid treatment [ 1 , 16 ]. In a review by R amamurthy et al. [ 43 ], pulse administration of i.v. methylprednisolone at a dose of 30 mg·kg −1 daily for 3 days every 4–6 weeks for 6–12 months was shown to improve survival. Other authors suggested doses of 10–30 mg·kg −1 daily for three consecutive days, repeated as a single-day monthly pulse [ 45 ] or monthly for three consecutive days [ 40 , 46 ]. In a review by C lement et al. [ 14 ], few cases were reported to benefit from the combination of oral prednisolone and i.v. methylprednisolone, being such simultaneous therapy suggested for patients with severe disease. Historically, pulsed i.v. corticosteroids were recommended for children with severe disease or when oral steroids failed [ 47 ]. Moreover, it was hypothesised that pulse therapy could prevent the downregulation of glucocorticoid receptors observed during daily oral treatment. Over time, i.v. therapy became preferred over daily oral steroids as it was shown to be at least as effective while causing fewer side-effects [ 38 , 48 ] such as hypertension, diabetes and bone demineralisation [ 49 ]. To date, no consensus has been reached on the optimal corticosteroid regimen or its duration in chILD. However, current practice often favours pulsed i.v. steroids for acute or deteriorating conditions and oral steroids for chronic therapy [ 41 , 50 ]. Close monitoring of clinical response and potential side-effects, such as through bone density scans, serial growth measurements and ophthalmological evaluations, remains essential [ 51 ]. In the absence of clear benefit, continuation of steroid treatment should be carefully reconsidered given the risk of significant adverse effects. Prolonged or high-dose corticosteroid requirements may warrant earlier consideration of referral for lung transplantation, particularly in patients refractory to therapy. Such decisions should be guided by comprehensive clinical, functional and radiological monitoring [ 52 ]. Hydroxychloroquine The antimalarial drug HCQ has historically been used in rheumatic diseases for its immunological effects by inhibiting T-cell function [ 50 ]. B en- Z vi et al . [ 53 ] reported that HCQ modulates immune responses by altering lysosomal activity, cytokine release and multiple signalling pathways, including T-/B-cell, Toll-like receptor and interleukin (IL) (IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22) regulation. HCQ has been reported in 50% of chILD cases as a steroid-sparing agent, even if it remained off-label for years, and its use based on clinical practice and case series [ 50 , 54 ]. In 2015 the European guidelines [ 1 ] reported the use of HCQ as a second-line therapy in patients with chILD suggesting a dose of 10 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 , reducible to 6.5 mg·kg −1 in children under 6 years of age to minimise side-effects. 54% of the clinicians who underwent the Delphi process also considered the opportunity to start HCQ as a first-line therapy in patients not ventilated (or close to ventilation) with mild stable chILD. Since the publication of these guidelines, in 2022 the first multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial assessing the efficacy of HCQ in chILD was released ( NCT02615938 ) [ 55 ]. A total of 35 patients with chronic diffuse parenchymal lung disease were recruited and no significant statistical difference was found between placebo and HCQ groups in terms of change in oxygenation, respiratory rate and the need for respiratory support. As for safety outcomes, HCQ (10 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 for the first week, followed by 6.5 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 ) was generally well tolerated, with no difference found in adverse events between placebo or HCQ [ 55 , 56 ]. Even considering the limitations of this trial, such as the small sample size and the population's heterogeneity, the result contrasted with previous literature, based on case series, where the positive response to HCQ was primarily a clinical impression, without any measurable outcome. Macrolides Initially briefly mentioned by C lement et al. [ 20 ], in the following years macrolides became a promising therapeutic option for chILD [ 14 ] due to their antibiotic, anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects. Azithromycin was demonstrated to inhibit collagen production and enhance apoptosis in idiopathic PF by disrupting lysosomal acidification and impairing autophagic flux. These effects, linked to altered lysosomal ATPase activity and increased lysosomal pH, highlighted a mechanism through which azithromycin may exert antifibrotic actions [ 57 ]. In European guidelines released in 2015 [ 1 ], azithromycin was recommended as a second-line drug at a dosage of 10 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 for 3 days per week with an expected response rate in 3 months. No preference over HCQ as a second-line treatment was established in nonventilated patients. In addition, azithromycin was indicated by 51% of the clinicians involved in the Delphi process as a possible monotherapy for mild stable chILD, likewise for HCQ. So far, evidence of their efficacy in chILD is still limited to few case reports and no clinical trial has been conducted [ 41 , 58 – 60 ]. Immunosuppressive agents Azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide or cyclosporine may be used as second-line therapy in chILD, considered as steroid-sparing agents or as add-on therapy in severe or rapidly progressive chILD [ 40 , 43 ]. A very limited number of studies provided recommendations for doses. C lement et al . [ 20 ] suggested azathioprine 2–3 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 , cyclophosphamide 1–1.5 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 , cyclosporine 6 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 and methotrexate 2.5–7.5 mg·kg −1 ·week −1 . No subsequent consensus or international guidelines addressing the dosages of immunosuppressive therapies have been published, leaving the decision to single centres. Lung transplant Lung transplant is considered the ultimate therapy for children with advanced-stage chILD, severe ILD unresponsive to other treatments or at high risk of mortality, such as alveolar capillary dysplasia [ 43 , 47 ]. Since 2013, ATS guidelines strongly recommended a prompt referral to a paediatric lung transplantation centre for infants with severe, life-threatening chILD diseases [ 16 ]. Initial reports showed the recurrence of ILDs and the risk of bronchiolitis obliterans in a very high percentage of long-term transplant recipients [ 47 ]. On the other hand, a study conducted by R ama et al . [ 61 ] revealed that lung transplantation outcomes are comparable in patients with chILD and recipients with other diagnoses. Recently, a retrospective review in 44 infants with genetic disorder of surfactant metabolism described substantial morbidities and mortality after lung transplantation [ 62 ]. Antifibrotic drugs PF may represent the end stage of ILD, although in children it is rarer than in adult patients [ 46 ]. CT-scoring systems for paediatric PF still need to be developed and validated [ 63 ]. Patterns of usual interstitial pneumonia, a form of progressive lung scarring, were described in children with variants of SP-C and ABCA3 (ATP-binding cassette subfamily A member 3) [ 46 , 64 , 65 ]. R ice et al . [ 29 ] examined histopathological pattern of lung biopsy in chILD, finding fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia in 2.1% of patients under 2 years of age and in 6.7% of patients aged 2−18 years. Compared to adults, children with PF seem to have fewer fibrotic lesions, characterised by greater cellular recruitment, less collagen accumulation and minimal parenchymal damage [ 66 ]. This suggests the potential of antifibrotic treatment, such as nintedanib and pirfenidone, which have already been approved in adults with idiopathic PF. Nintedanib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that inhibits growth factors involved in the development of PF (platelet-derived, fibroblast and vascular endothelial growth factors), while pirfenidone has anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic properties reducing fibroblast activity [ 50 ]. Both drugs have been shown to reduce disease progression and slow the rate of decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) in adults with IPF [ 41 , 67 , 68 ] and nintedanib also decreased the rate of pulmonary deterioration in adults with ILD that progress despite appropriate treatment [ 41 ]. A phase 2, multicentre, placebo-controlled clinical trial (InPedILD trial: NCT04093024 ) was recently published evaluating nintedanib in children and adolescents with fibrosing ILD [ 69 , 70 ]. The authors demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and reported a stabilisation of FVC and O 2 saturation at rest in the nintedanib group while the same parameters showed a decline in the placebo group over 24 weeks, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to limited sample size and trial duration. M aher et al . [ 71 ], using a Bayesian statistical model that incorporated adult data on the effects of nintedanib on FVC, estimated an effect in children and adolescents of 1.63% predicted over 24 weeks, with a 95.5% probability of superiority over placebo. Considering these relevant results, an open-label extension study on the long-term safety and tolerability of nintedanib in children and adolescents with ILD is currently recruiting ( NCT05285982 ) [ 72 ]. Data on the use of pirfenidone in the paediatric population are scarce and no clinical trials have been conducted. To date, only a few case reports on this drug in paediatric PF have been published, but they did not demonstrate a clear benefit in chILD with PF, likely due to significant confounding factors as other therapies concomitant use. Although no definitive proof of efficacy can be drawn, the reports suggested that pirfenidone was generally well-tolerated, with gastrointestinal side effects being the most common [ 73 , 74 ]. Emerging treatments In the last few years, an increasing interest has been directed towards cellular and gene therapy for several lung diseases, including ILD. As for cellular therapy, mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) show considerable promise due to their regenerative, antifibrotic and immunomodulatory properties [ 75 , 76 ]. These effects have been described also on lung tissue, in particular in bleomycin-induced preclinical models of fibrosis, in which adipose tissue-derived MSCs significantly reduce collagen deposition and scar formation compared to controls [ 41 , 76 – 79 ]. In adults, a phase 1b trial based on endobronchial infusion of autologous adipose tissue derived MSCs confirmed their safety in IPF treatment. Other preclinical studies have been published, with encouraging results about the role of adipose tissue or bone marrow-derived MSCs in contrasting or preventing PF. In vitro studies on the use of induced pluripotent stem cells were also promising for correcting surfactant protein genes variants. Regarding clinical studies, we identified only one clinical report on the use of MSCs as a rescue therapy for lung disease associated with the filamin A (FLNA) gene mutation in an 18-month-old child. No acute adverse events were observed. Following the infusion, the child's respiratory condition improved, leading to reduced dependence on mechanical ventilation. As for gene therapy, gene-based therapies have been recently applied in chILD animal models based on monogenic defects [ 80 ]. Adeno-associated virus, lentiviral and adenoviral vectors have been proposed as delivery mechanisms for both gene addition or gene-editing approaches for surfactant disorders associated with pathogenic variants in SP-B, SP-C and ABCA3 [ 81 ]. This research field is quite promising, however the possible translation of these preclinical studies in murine models in the paediatric population is still unknown [ 82 ]. Synthetic androgen therapy represents one of the most advanced experimental approaches currently under investigation for telomere-related gene (TRG) disorders [ 83 , 84 ]. Early studies demonstrated that danazol could partially reverse telomere shortening and improve haematologic parameters in patients with TRG variants, although its long-term use has been limited by hepatic toxicity [ 85 ]. More recent data suggest that earlier initiation of therapy and the use of less hepatotoxic analogues such as nandrolone may offer a safer and potentially more effective strategy to mitigate fibrosis progression [ 85 ]. Ongoing prospective clinical trials (TELO-SCOPE, NCT04638517 , ANDROTELO, NCT03710356 ) are expected to provide critical evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of androgen-based therapies in patients with ILD and TRG variants [ 85 ]. Treatment of specific conditions Below, we describe the most commonly used therapies for chILD, categorising them by specific conditions and highlighting data from recent case reports, case series and the latest findings in preclinical research. Neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia of infancy (NEHI) NEHI is a form of chILD previously named persistent tachypnoea of infancy, since it presents with insidious onset of tachypnoea, retractions, crackles and hypoxaemia in infants during the first months of life. In a recent retrospective study at a Polish referral centre on 275 children with chILD, NEHI has been described as the most frequent diagnosis (52.4%) [ 86 ]. Its aetiology is still undefined, but lung biopsies of children with NEHI found increased numbers of neuroendocrine cells in the airways. Diagnosis is made combining characteristic HRCT findings with a suspicious clinical context [ 87 ]. A recent European multicentre retrospective study involving 378 children from 17 countries provided the largest overview to date of NEHI [ 88 ]. The study highlighted that diagnosis typically occurs around 9 months of age and is primarily based on characteristic clinical features, such as tachypnoea, retractions, crackles, hypoxaemia and failure to thrive, together with HRCT findings. Lung biopsy, confirming pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia in about half of the cases, was performed in only one-quarter of patients, with a declining frequency over time and variability across countries. Genetic testing and other ancillary investigations were infrequently used and inconsistently applied. Overall, the study [ 88 ] underscores marked heterogeneity in diagnostic strategies across Europe and emphasises the urgent need for standardised guidelines for the evaluation and diagnosis of persistent tachypnea of infancy/NEHI. No standardised therapeutic guidelines are available. In a recent French nationwide observational study, which include patients with NEHI from French hospitals with a paediatric rare lung disease centre [ 89 ], initial treatments were oxygen (83.6%) and i.v. methylprednisolone pulses (83.3%) followed by long-term azithromycin (70.2%). Less frequently French paediatric pulmonologists prescribe HCQ (36.2%), inhaled steroids (44.7%) and inhaled beta-2 agonists (31.2%). Several case reports and case series have described treatment and outcomes in children with NEHI, with conflicting results ( table 2 ). The cornerstone of management remains oxygen therapy, along with nutritional support and infection prevention, followed by other medications with a low level of evidence [ 90 , 92 , 97 ]. This is likely due to evidence suggesting that clinical improvement in infants tends to occur with age, particularly after 2 years of age. Emerging evidence suggests that NEHI represents a pulmonary dysmaturation syndrome, characterised by persistent bombesin-positive cells from intrauterine life [ 98 ]. These cells are high at mid-gestation and decline by birth to the low levels seen in adulthood [ 90 ]. B ush [ 3 ] recently suggested adopting a supportive treatment approach for NEHI, focusing on oxygen and nutritional therapy. In order to make generalised recommendations for NEHI treatment, further studies and control trials are urgently needed. Pulmonary interstitial glycogenosis (PIG) PIG is a rare chILD of unknown aetiology. Diagnosis can be made on lung biopsy with intracellular glycogen storage and thickening of interalveolar septae [ 99 ]. Infants typically present respiratory distress and hypoxaemia before 9 months of life, and often gradually improve over time [ 100 ]. When PIG is associated with structural heart disease, pulmonary hypertension and/or alveolar simplification, it has been linked to poor prognosis, persistent symptoms or death [ 101 ]. No clinical consensus guidelines or extensive reviews have defined a shared therapeutic approach for PIG, which is mainly based on case reports describing the use of systemic corticosteroid. A better understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms would lead to new targeted therapies [ 102 ]. A retrospective multicentre study [ 103 ] reported 11 children with PIG treated with either pulse (methylprednisolone 10 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 for 3 days or prednisolone 50 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 for 4 days) or continuous systemic glucocorticoids (2 mg·kg −1 ·day −1 ), of whom four showed significant improvement during a median follow-up of 3 years, while one child died. In a case series by L iptzin et al. [ 101 ], among 24 patients with PIG, 22 patients received systemic corticosteroids, with three patients (13.6%) showing a marked clinical response. In 2018, a commentary [ 104 ] recommended a mild, short course of glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 2 mg·kg −1 every 6 h for 5 days), as used in the case described by D eutsch et al . [ 105 ]. Based on the current evidence, case reports and case series have provided conflicting results regarding the efficacy of corticosteroids in children with PIG and further evaluated through prospective controlled trials [ 104 ]. Genetic surfactant disorder The inborn genetic errors of surfactant metabolism include variants in five genes encoding SP-C, SP-B, thyroid transcription factor 1/NK2 homeobox 1 (TTF-1/NKX2.1) and ABCA3, with different timing and severity of presentation depending on the variant [ 106 ]. SP-C disorder (autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance) can present at various and with variable clinical manifestations [ 107 , 108 ]. SP-C variants may be asymptomatic or present with tachypnoea, hypoxaemia, persistent cough and failure to thrive [ 108 ]. SP-B disorder (autosomal recessive inheritance) is considered to be the rarest genetic surfactant dysfunction disorder. This condition typically presents in full-term infants with diffuse lung disease that rapidly progresses and results in respiratory failure and death within the first 3–6 months of life [ 82 ]. ABCA3 deficiency (autosomal recessive inheritance) is the most common cause of SP disorder. Clinically, it can be as severe as SP-B disorder or present with subacute progressive lung disease during childhood, with a notable genotype–phenotype correlation [ 107 ]. Patients with NKX2.1-related disease classically present with a triad of neurological dysfunction, hypothyroidism and lung disease. The lung involvement causes respiratory distress in neonatal period or early infancy even if chronic phenotypes in adults are also described [ 109 ]. The most common, noninvasive therapeutic strategy for infants with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant disorder is exogenous surfactant replacement. This leads to a transient improvement in oxygen requirements lasting a few hours, although the response diminishes over time [ 110 ]. Anti-inflammatory medications, which include corticosteroids, HCQ and azithromycin, have also been applied with limited efficacy [ 82 ]. Despite its obvious limitations, lung transplantation remains the definitive treatment option for progressive respiratory failure among infants and children [ 82 , 111 , 112 ]. Recent data indicate that lung transplantation in children with chILD is associated with favourable mid-term survival outcomes comparable to those observed in other paediatric indications, such as cystic fibrosis and pulmonary hypertension, despite higher pretransplant morbidity in infants with early-onset disease [ 111 , 112 ]. In this context, international consensus guidelines emphasise the importance of timely referral and careful candidate selection to optimise outcomes and address the clinical and ethical challenges inherent to paediatric lung transplantation [ 111 ]. Currently, gene therapy remains the most promising therapeutic strategy for genetic disorders of surfactant dysfunction [ 82 ]. As described in table 3 , the most frequently used treatments include HCQ, systemic steroids ( i.v. pulse methylprednisolone and oral prednisolone) and azithromycin, with lung transplantation being less common and considered only in cases with a progressive worsening of symptoms [ 113 – 117 ]. Recently, pirfenidone has been reported as an additional therapy to slow disease progression and clinical decline [ 73 ]. Moreover, gene editing for the SP-C variant has been investigated using intra-amniotic delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 during fetal development in a mouse model. This approach resulted in the inactivation of the mutant SFTPC gene, leading to improved lung morphology and increased postnatal survival in mice [ 121 ]. Currently, no clear guidelines are available; therefore, the use of different medications for SP-C disorder is largely based on the practice and experience of individual centres. Surfactant protein B disorder Due to the extreme rarity of SP-B disorder, only a few studies investigated the potential therapeutic approaches. These studies have primarily focused on gene addition [ 122 , 123 ] and gene-editing strategies [ 124 , 125 ], suggesting that restoring SP-B expression in alveolar epithelial type II cells could correct the phenotypic defect both in vitro and in vivo . Recent studies demonstrate that optimised gene therapy based on adeno-associated viruses can restore surfactant homeostasis and markedly prolong survival in SP-B-deficient mouse models, highlighting strong translational potential for this otherwise lethal disease [ 126 , 127 ]. As described in table 4 , the most frequent treatments used were HCQ, prednisolone and/or methylprednisolone, and azithromycin. Y ang et al . [ 130 ] generated evidence for an ABCA3 variant-dependent impact of HCQ in vitro and showed a direct correlation with the HCQ response in vivo . Moreover, lung transplant has been reported in one clinical case [ 129 ]. New treatment strategies have been recently investigated in vitro models, such as cyclosporin A [ 138 ], identified and validated as a potential corrector for some specific ABCA3 variants by enabling ABCA3 maturation to wild-type levels. Currently, there is no clear evidence on the best therapeutic approach and treatment choices rely on each centre's experience. This limited options for ABCA3 deficiency may stem from an incomplete understanding of its pathogenesis. Recently, S un et al . [ 140 ] developed an in vitro disease model using alveolar type II epithelial cells from patients with ABCA3 variants. Through functional, proteomic, lipidomic and transcriptomic analyses, they confirmed surfactant dysfunction due to reduced phospholipid secretion and unexpectedly increased NF-κB signalling, leading to inflammatory cytokine release. Another area of preclinical research with promising results refers to the potential application of drugs used in cystic fibrosis, known as correctors, for conditions where protein misfolding leads to loss of function, such as with ABCA3 gene variants [ 141 ]. The rationale is based on the similarities between the lipid transporter ABCA3 and the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, both of which are ABC transporters [ 41 ]. NK2 homeobox 1 variants N attes et al. [ 142 ] retrospectively described the clinical presentation, treatment modalities and outcome in 16 patients with heterozygous NKX2-1 variant associated with chronic lung disease. All symptomatic ILD patients (n=12) benefited from a treatment consisting of steroids, azithromycin (n=9) and/or HCQ (n=4). The median follow-up was 36 months (interquartile range 24.0–71.5). One patient died of respiratory failure at 18 months and another is waiting for lung transplantation. Conclusions In conclusion, we examined the therapeutic approach in chILD, from supportive care during the diagnostic process to targeted treatments prescribed once the cause of the disease is identified ( table S1 ). Our systematic review confirmed the relevant role of oxygen therapy, ventilation support, proper nutrition, immunisations and environmental precautions in managing chILD, along with prophylaxis against infections and comprehensive family-centred care. Corticosteroids remain a key treatment, with oral prednisolone or pulsed i.v. methylprednisolone commonly used to reduce inflammation and slower disease progression. HCQ is recommended as second-line therapy, with some clinicians considering it for first-line use. However, its role remains debated, as a 2022 multicentre trial found no significant benefit over placebo. No consensus or international guidelines are available for immunosuppressive therapies, macrolides and antifibrotic agents. Lung transplantation remains the definitive treatment option for progressive respiratory failure. Cellular and gene therapies are emerging as promising approaches for treating chILD, with MSCs showing regenerative and antifibrotic potential and gene-based therapies, including viral vector delivery for surfactant disorders, though translation from preclinical models to paediatric patients still has a long journey ahead. Points for clinical practice Oxygen therapy, ventilation support, proper nutrition, immunisations and environmental precautions have a relevant role, along with prophylaxis against infections and comprehensive family-centred care. Corticosteroids remain a key treatment, with oral prednisolone or pulsed i.v. methylprednisolone, while HCQ is recommended as second-line therapy. No consensus or international guidelines are available for immunosuppressive therapies, macrolides and antifibrotic agents. Lung transplantation remains the definitive treatment option for progressive respiratory failure. Footnotes Provenance: Submitted article, peer reviewed. documents.title: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation for acute asthma in children.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Asthma is one of the most common reasons for hospital admission among children, with significant economic burden and impact on quality of life. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) is increasingly used in the care of children with acute asthma, although the evidence supporting it is weak, and clinical guidelines do not offer any recommendations on its routine use. However, NPPV might be an effective way to improve outcomes for some children with asthma. A previous review did not demonstrate a clear benefit, but was limited by few studies with small sample sizes. This is an update of the previous review.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of NPPV as an add-on therapy to usual care (e.g. bronchodilators and corticosteroids) in children (< 18 years) with acute asthma.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase. We also conducted a search of ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO ICTRP. We searched all databases from their inception to March 2023, with no restrictions on language of publication.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised clinical trials (RCTs) assessing NPPV as add-on therapy to usual care versus usual care for children hospitalised for acute asthma exacerbations.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We used standard Cochrane methods.
MAIN RESULTS: We included three RCTs randomising 60 children with acute asthma to NPPV and 60 children to control. All included trials assessed the effects of bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) for acute asthma in a paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) setting. None of the trials used continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). The controls received standard care. The median age of children ranged from three to six years, and asthma severity ranged from moderate to severe. Our primary outcome measures were all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, and asthma symptom score. Secondary outcomes were non-serious adverse events, health-related quality of life, arterial blood gases and pH, pneumonia, cost, and PICU length of stay. None of the trials reported any deaths or serious adverse events (except one trial that reported intubation rate). Two trials reported asthma symptom score, each demonstrating reductions in asthma symptoms in the BiPAP group. In one trial, the asthma symptom score was (mean difference (MD) -2.50, 95% confidence interval (CI) -4.70 to -0.30, P = 0.03; 19 children) lower in the BiPAP group. In the other trial, a cross-over trial, BiPAP was associated with a lower mean asthma symptom score (MD -3.7; 16 children; very low certainty evidence) before cross-over, but investigators did not report a standard deviation, and it could not be estimated from the first phase of the trial before cross-over. The reduction in both trials was above our predefined minimal important difference. Overall, NPPV with standard care may reduce asthma symptom score compared to standard care alone, but the evidence is very uncertain. The only reported serious adverse event was intubation rate in one trial. The trial had an intubation rate of 40% and showed that BiPAP may result in a large reduction in intubation rate (risk ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.95; 78 children), but the evidence is very uncertain. Post hoc analysis showed that BiPAP may result in a slight decrease in length of PICU stay (MD -0.87 day, 95% CI -1.52 to -0.22; 100 children), but the evidence is very uncertain. Meta-analysis or Trial Sequential Analysis was not possible because of insufficient reporting and different scoring systems. All three trials had high risk of bias with serious imprecision of results, leading to very low certainty of evidence.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: The currently available evidence for NNPV is uncertain. NPPV may lead to an improvement in asthma symptom score, decreased intubation rate, and slightly shorter PICU stay; however, the evidence is of very low certainty. Larger RCTs with low risk of bias are warranted.

documents.title: Risk factors for complications of Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in hospitalized children in China: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MPP) is a common respiratory disease in children. Some patients may develop long-term respiratory issues such as chronic cough and wheezing due to complications. These complications increase the health burden for children with MPP, highlighting the need to understand their risk factors in order to improve disease prognosis. This study aims to assess the risk factors for complications in hospitalized children with MPP in China.
METHODS: A comprehensive review of Chinese and English databases was conducted up to April 2024 to retrieve studies focusing on complications in hospitalized children with MPP. Pooled effect sizes were calculated using random-effects or fixed-effects models. Statistical analyses were performed using R software and RevMan 5.3.
RESULTS: This meta-analysis encompassed a total of 17 studies. We analyzed multiple risk factors associated with complications, including prolonged fever (OR: 3.79, aOR: 1.64), pleural effusion (OR: 3.71, aOR: 6.70), extensive lung infiltration (OR: 5.52, aOR: 3.57), ≥ 2/3 consolidation in a single lung lobe (OR: 4.29, aOR: 4.52), right upper lung lesion (OR: 4.84, aOR: 3.57), extrapulmonary manifestations (OR: 3.20, aOR: 1.89), hypoxemia (OR: 7.58, aOR: 12.43), delayed administration of glucocorticoids (OR: 7.93, aOR: 6.67), and delayed administration of macrolides (OR: 2.75, aOR: 3.84).
CONCLUSION: Hospitalized children with SMPP and RMPP may have a higher risk of complications, and it is important to identify risk factors early and provide appropriate treatment to minimize complications. The current level of evidence is relatively low and may not accurately reflect the actual clinical situation in China. Further high-quality studies are needed to validate and clarify these findings.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Our protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42024534397).
documents.conclusions: Hospitalized children with SMPP and RMPP may have a higher risk of complications, and it is important to identify risk factors early and provide appropriate treatment to minimize complications. The current level of evidence is relatively low and may not accurately reflect the actual clinical situation in China. Further high-quality studies are needed to validate and clarify these findings.

Introduction Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) is a cell wall-free prokaryote capable of causing both upper and lower respiratory infections. Epidemiological studies indicate that MP infections affect all age groups, with a higher prevalence among children [ 1 ]. Given the fact that children's bodies are in a stage of rapid development and their immune systems are insufficiently mature, they are more vulnerable to MP infections [ 2 ]. MP is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in children [ 3 ], responsible for approximately 40% of CAP cases attributed to Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MPP) from MP infection [ 4 , 5 ]. MPP exhibits an epidemic peak every 3–7 years, and the regional outbreaks in China since last autumn have exacerbated the national public health burden [ 6 , 7 ]. Previous studies reported that some children with MPP may develop severe complications, such as bronchiolitis obliterans, bronchiectasis, atelectasis, and myocardial damage [ 8 – 11 ]. These complications are closely related to severe mycoplasma pneumonia (SMPP) and refractory mycoplasma pneumonia (RMPP). SMPP is primarily determined based on symptoms and clinical progression, while RMPP emphasizes the lack of response to initial therapy. Specifically, RMPP is characterized by persistent fever, worsening clinical symptoms, and deteriorating pulmonary imaging despite macrolide treatment lasting 7 days or longer [ 12 ]. In recent years, there has been increasing attention to cases of severe mycoplasma pneumonia (SMPP) and refractory mycoplasma pneumonia (RMPP) [ 13 , 14 ], and how to effectively prevent complications has become a critical issue in the management of MPP [ 15 ]. Among these complications, considerable attention is given to bronchiolitis obliterans and bronchitis obliterans [ 16 – 18 ]. Children with MPP are at heightened risk of developing post-infectious bronchiolitis obliterans, second only to those infected with adenovirus [ 19 ]. Bronchiolitis obliterans is characterized primarily by wheezing, which reflects inflammatory damage and fibrotic changes in the small airways, leading to narrowing or complete occlusion of the airway lumen [ 20 ]. Bronchitis obliterans presents as persistent cough and dyspnoea, with features including segmental and sub-segmental bronchial obstruction, fibrous tissue proliferation, lung collapse, and bronchiectasis [ 15 , 21 ]. Previous studies have confirmed that MPP can result in residual chronic cough, wheezing, restrictive lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, and persistent small airway dysfunction [ 22 – 24 ]. The complications of MPP can persist for more than 6 months, closely linked to these long-term respiratory issues, posing a significant threat to children's health and severely impacting their quality of life after discharge. Therefore, preventing these complications is crucial for improving the prognosis of children affected by MPP. A thorough understanding of the risk factors for complications aids in the development of effective prevention strategies. Although clinicians and researchers have increasingly focused on MPP complications in recent years, leading to many clinical studies, the published research on this topic comes mainly from individual research centers. This has led to variations in the data, creating uncertainty about the clinical applicability of the findings. Therefore, this study aims to systematically review the literature on complications associated with MPP, conduct a meta-analysis to assess high-risk populations and primary risk factors, and provide recommendations for complication prevention based on the findings. Methods This study was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 25 ]. The detailed information of our protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42024534397). Search strategy We searched Chinese electronic databases including China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), VIP Information, Wanfang Data Knowledge Service Platform, Chinese Biomedical Literature Service System (SionMed), as well as major international databases such as PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Our objective was to review observational studies related to complications of MPP in hospitalized children published in China from the establishment of the database until April 2024. The search terms were selected from PubMed’s MeSH thesaurus and included 'Mycoplasma pneumonia', 'complications', 'sequelae', and 'child'. Boolean operators were used to merge subject terms and free-text phrases, creating search strings tailored to the unique characteristics of each respective database. Two researchers (ZW and YP) conducted independent searches simultaneously, with any discrepancies resolved by consensus with a third researcher (XL). Additionally, we reviewed the references of included studies to supplement our search and ensure comprehensive literature retrieval. No language restrictions were applied to the included literature, and non-Chinese publications were translated for comprehension. The full search strategy is detailed in Additional file 1. Eligibility criteria This review exclusively included observational studies, specifically case–control and cohort studies. To be eligible, studies should be conducted in China and recruited hospitalized children diagnosed with MPP. No restrictions based on disease severity were imposed, ensuring a comprehensive examination across different severities. The complications reported in these studies were required to be related to the respiratory issues caused by MPP. Given the studies' origin in China, we defined these complications based on the latest 'Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of Mycoplasma Pneumonae Pneumonia in Children (2023 Edition)' issued by the National Health Commission of the People's Republic of China [ 12 ]. Additionally, included studies were required to provide original data suitable for calculating the odds ratios for risk factors associated with MPP complications. We excluded case reports, conference abstracts, inaccessible dissertations, and duplicated publications from our review. Studies were also excluded if their classification of complications from MPP did not align with established guidelines. Additionally, studies with incomplete data or significant errors were excluded. Data extraction The literature screening and data extraction were independently conducted by two researchers (ZW and YP). Initially, articles were screened based on titles and abstracts, followed by a full-text evaluation against predetermined selection criteria to identify eligible studies and extract data. In cases where different studies involved the same group of subjects, priority was given to the study with the most comprehensive dataset. Throughout each phase, both researchers cross-checked their screening results, with a third researcher (XL) responsible for resolving any discrepancies. The following data were extracted: study characteristics (first author, publication year, study design), sample size, number of complications cases, basic participant information (severity of MPP, median age, province), and risk factors [definition, odds ratios (ORs), and/or adjusted ORs with respective 95% confidence intervals (95% CI)]. For ease of grouping in statistical analysis, we categorized the provinces where studies were conducted into six regions based on geographical location: North China, Northeast China, South Central China, Southwest China, East China, and Northwest China. Quality assessment The methodological quality of case–control and cohort studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ 26 ], which evaluates the selection of study participants, comparability between groups, and assessment of exposure or outcome. The maximum score for study was 9 points, with a score of 7–9 points indicated high quality. We did not exclude studies based on the quality assessment results. Statistical analysis Our initial assessment revealed a significant variation in the complication rates, largely influenced by the severity of MPP. To assess the impact of MPP severity on the risk of complications, we categorized the studies included in our analysis into two groups based on participant severity: hospitalized children with MPP across all severity levels, and those with SMPP/RMPP. We separately pooled the proportions of children with complications in different groups and conducted preliminary comparisons based on the geographical locations of the institutions and the participants' ages. In this meta-analysis, we synthesized the ORs and adjusted ORs of risk factors investigated in at least two studies using multivariable designs. Definitions of the same risk factor were ensured to be consistent across all included studies. The heterogeneity was quantified and tested using I 2 and Q statistic (α = 0.1). If heterogeneity was deemed acceptable (P > 0.10 and I 2 ≤ 50%), a fixed-effects model was applied; otherwise, a random-effects model was used, followed by an exploration of potential sources of heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate the impact of individual studies on the overall result stability. In addition, we generated funnel plots and employed Egger’s and Begg’s tests to quantify the risk of publication bias. All statistical analyses were performed using the meta package in R 4.4.0 and RevMan 5.3. Results Search results We initially retrieved 3154 relevant records through our literature search. After removing duplicates, we reviewed the titles and abstracts of 2354 records and conducted full-text evaluations of the remaining 67. Ultimately, only 17 studies that met the inclusion criteria were included in the final review. The flowchart illustrating the literature screening process is presented in Fig. 1 . The complete list of included studies can be found in Additional file 2. Fig. 1 The study selection process Characteristics of the studies The characteristics of the 17 included studies are summarized in Table 1 . This systematic review comprised 16 case–control studies[ 17 , 27 – 41 ] and 1 cohort study [ 42 ], all published between 2008 and 2023, involving 8751 Chinese hospitalized children with MPP. Among these studies, 11 focused on hospitalized children with MPP across all severity levels, while 6 investigated children with SMPP or RMPP. The median age of participants across all studies ranged from 1.2 to 8.2 years. Geographically, the studies were distributed as follows: 2 from North China; 3 from East China; 4 each from Northeast China, South Central China and Southwest China; and no studies were conducted in Northwest China. Quality assessment of the literature indicated 6 studies were of high quality, with detailed NOS scores provided in Additional file 3. We analyzed both unadjusted and adjusted ORs for 10 factors. Among all factors, four radiographic manifestations showed statistically significant associations with complications: pleural effusion [OR: 3.71(95%CI: 1.85–7.43), p = 0.0002; aOR: 6.70(95%CI: 3.60–12.45), p < 0.00001], extensive infiltration shadow in the lung [OR: 5.52(95%CI: 3.82–7.98), p < 0.00001; aOR: 3.57(95%CI: 2.58–4.94), p < 0.00001], ≥ 2/3 consolidation in a single lung lobe [OR: 4.29(95%CI: 1.48–12.39), p = 0.007; aOR: 4.52(95%CI: 1.94–10.52), p = 0.0005], and right upper lung lesion [OR: 4.84(95%CI: 3.35–7.00), p < 0.00001; aOR: 3.57(95%CI: 2.58–4.94), p < 0.00001]. Prolonged fever (≥ 10 days) [OR: 3.79(95%CI: 2.69–5.34), p < 0.00001; aOR: 1.64(95%CI: 1.16–2.30), p = 0.005], extrapulmonary manifestations [OR: 3.20(95%CI: 2.12–4.85), p < 0.00001; aOR: 1.89(95%CI: 1.08–3.30), p = 0.03], and hypoxemia [OR: 7.58(95%CI: 3.49–16.47), p < 0.00001; aOR: 12.43(95%CI: 1.09–141.75), p = 0.04] were identified as risk factors for complications. Two treatment-related factors also increased the risk of complications: delayed use of macrolides [OR: 2.75(95%CI: 1.66–4.55), p < 0.0001; aOR: 3.84(95%CI: 1.76–8.38), p = 0.0007] and delayed use of glucocorticoids [OR: 7.93(95%CI: 4.90–12.84), p < 0.00001; aOR: 6.67(95%CI: 2.44–18.26), p = 0.0002]. However, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) [OR: 2.64(95%CI: 0.34–20.56), p = 0.35; aOR: 1.38(95%CI: 0.87–2.18), p = 0.17] showed no significant correlation with complications. A total of 17 studies that met our inclusion criteria were used for the analysis. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we categorized pediatric cases of MPP based on disease severity, and conducted a preliminary comparison of complication rates by aggregating the proportion of children with complications reported in the included studies. The result indicate that severe illness correlates with a heightened risk of complications. A previous systematic review compared the risk of complications between hospitalized and non-hospitalized children with pneumonia [ 22 ]. In this study, we specifically focused on hospitalized children infected with MP, thereby minimizing the impact of pathogen diversity on the results. It is widely acknowledged that the pathogenic mechanisms of MP involve both direct tissue damage and immune-mediated injury [ 43 ]. Furthermore, MP can evade phagocytosis by host immune cells through its immune evasion mechanisms, promoting prolonged survival in the body and contributing to chronic infection [ 44 ]. Airway remodeling and fibrotic changes may result from tissue damage caused by recurrent infections and sustained inflammation, potentially causing complications such as bronchiectasis, bronchitis obliterans, and bronchiolitis obliterans [ 45 , 46 ]. Excessive immune response is also considered a contributing factor to the development of complications [ 47 ]. The presence of aberrant immune responses and stronger inflammatory reactions in children with SMPP or RMPP may explain their heightened risk of complications [ 48 , 49 ]. Disparities in reported complication rates among research institutions in various regions may stem from factors such as climate conditions, proportion of severe cases, and duration of illness in patients [ 5 , 50 ]. However, due to the limited number of included studies, the results from regional subgroups may not adequately reflect the occurrence of complications in hospitalized children with MPP in those regions. Previous studies suggested that MP infection is more prevalent in children aged 5 years or older compared to younger children [ 51 ]. Nevertheless, in this study, the complication rate among hospitalized children with MPP was similar across age groups, including those aged 5 years and older and those under 5 years. This study does not provide evidence to suggest that there are differences in the risk of complications among children with MPP across different age groups. By aggregating the risk of different types of complications, we found that the risk of atelectasis in hospitalized children with MPP is higher than that of other complications reported. Bronchitis obliterans was reported only in children with SMPP/RMPP, which prevents an assessment of its overall risk in hospitalized children with MPP. Therefore, it was excluded from the comparison. Delayed resolution of atelectasis and persistent atelectasis can lead to prolonged respiratory issues [ 52 , 53 ]. However, for most MPP patients, atelectasis can recover after treatment with macrolide antibiotics, corticosteroids, bronchoalveolar lavage, etc. [ 54 ]. Due to limited information provided in the study, we may have aggregated children with persistent atelectasis and those with favorable prognosis of atelectasis. Bronchitis obliterans is a severe obstructive pulmonary disease [ 55 ]. In a Korean study of 150 hospitalized children with MPP, 18 cases developed bronchitis obliterans [ 18 ], which differs from the rates reported in the studies included in this paper. This discrepancy may be related to factors such as regional differences. Bronchiectasis is traditionally viewed as irreversible airway dilatation resulting from a vicious cycle of inflammation and recurrent infections. However, several studies suggested that bronchiectasis attributed to MP infection can resolve [ 15 ], described as ‘pseudo bronchiectasis’ or ‘functional bronchiectasis’. Some researchers speculated that pseudo bronchiectasis may represent an early reversible stage of bronchiectasis progression or could alternatively signify a distinct clinical entity or a misinterpretation of radiological findings. Therefore, confirming bronchiectasis diagnosis at least 6 months after the infection resolution is crucial [ 56 , 57 ]. Some studies reviewed here did not specify the exact timing of bronchiectasis diagnosis; hence the possibility of pseudo-bronchiectasis in these cases cannot be ruled out. This study evaluated multiple risk factors associated with complications in children with MPP based on meta-analysis. The development of complications is strongly linked to chronic infection-induced tissue inflammation and damage, as well as abnormal immune responses. Pleural effusion, indicative of severe local inflammation, emerged as a significant risk factor for MPP complications. According to Kim et al., pediatric patients treated with immunoregulatory agents who developed pleural effusion exhibited earlier resolution of fever compared to those without, suggesting a potential link between pleural effusion and excessive immune response [ 58 ]. Similarly, Narita et al. detected MP genomes and elevated IL-8 levels in the pleural effusion of pediatric patients with prolonged chest X-ray abnormalities post-MP infection [ 59 ]. The persistence of fever and extrapulmonary manifestations in pediatric patients implied ongoing inflammatory responses and heightened immune reactions, contributing to an increased risk of complications. Hypoxemia was another risk factor for complications. Studies showed that MPP patients experiencing hypoxemia demonstrate intensified immune-inflammatory responses [ 60 ]. Failure to promptly address hypoxia can worsen lung damage and heighten the risk of complications. Consolidation involving ≥ 2/3 of a single lung lobe was an independent risk factor for complications and served as a pivotal diagnostic criterion for SMPP. Early bronchial mucus plug formation exists in some pediatric patients experiencing complications such as bronchitis obliterans. However, due to variations in the implementation of bronchoscopy among hospitals, the presence of ≥ 2/3 consolidation in a single lung lobe serves as a practical marker for identifying mucus plug formation. Furthermore, radiological manifestations of large pulmonary infiltrates and lesions in the right upper lung correlated with the complications. Macrolide antibiotics are the primary choice for treating MP infections, while glucocorticoids, known for their anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressive effects, are frequently used as adjunctive therapy in MPP treatment. Delaying the initiation of macrolides and glucocorticoids increased the risk of developing complications. Consistent with this finding, children diagnosed with macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MRMP), which shows reduced responsiveness to treatment, often experience prolonged fever duration, severe radiographic manifestations, and heightened risks of complications [ 52 ]. Another study suggested that delayed effective antibiotic treatment and macrolide resistance play equally significant roles in prolonging the course of MPP [ 61 ]. In such cases, glucocorticoids are necessary to manage inflammation and promote fever reduction. Therefore, timely administration of macrolide antibiotics and glucocorticoids is crucial in MPP treatment to prevent complications. A study from Spain found that hypoxemia, neurological symptoms, and a history of prematurity are risk factors for ICU admission in children with MPP. The study also explained the association between the high use of steroids and the risk of severe disease [ 62 ]. Complications are influenced by the severity, and the risk factors associated with severe cases also provide valuable insights for the prevention of complications. As far as our knowledge extends, this study represents the first systematic review and meta-analysis consolidating data on the risk factors for complications among hospitalized children with MPP in China. We employed a comprehensive search strategy across both Chinese and English databases and implemented a dual-review process to ensure extensive coverage of currently published studies related to complications in children with MPP. Based on the severity of MPP in children, we conducted grouped discussions on the complication rates, highlighting an increased risk among those with SMPP or RMPP. Regarding the risk factors, we compared ORs with adjusted ORs provided in studies employing multivariable designs to offer a more reliable comprehensive assessment. There were several limitations in our study. Firstly, although our results suggested that children with SMPP and RMPP may face a higher risk of complications, the proportion of severe and refractory cases in certain studies included in this review was unknown. Considering that the included studies only reported the proportion of children with complications among the cases treated, this proportion is influenced by the overall severity of the cases, and any selection bias cannot be determined. Therefore, we believe that the pooled complication rate in this study does not accurately reflect the true clinical incidence of complications in MPP, and the results should be interpreted with caution. Secondly, there was a limited amount of research on complications associated with MPP, with Northwest China and some provinces in the other regions lacking analyzable data. Moreover, insufficient reporting on gender characteristics, disease course, and other relevant details in children with MPP complications hindered further subgroup analyses to assess clinical heterogeneity of complication rate. Thirdly, during risk factor analysis, we observed wide confidence intervals and significant heterogeneity in hypoxaemia, potentially impacting the reliability of the findings. Fourth, this research may only report respiratory complications due to the limitations of the treatment protocols and risk factors in the original studies, which may not include major complications from other systems. Lastly, although integrative treatments combining traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and Western medicine are increasingly used in Chinese hospitals and have shown promising outcomes for MPP, this systematic review lacks sufficient data on relevant risk factors, which limits its ability to provide robust evidence supporting the efficacy of such integrative approaches. Given these limitations, we advocate for future high-quality, large-scale, multicenter studies from diverse regions to assess the incidence and risk factors of complications associated with MPP. To comprehensively understand the risk of MPP complications across all populations, it is essential to separately examine complication rates in children with mild, severe, and refractory MPP in future studies. Due to the close association between complication occurrence and the severity of MPP, we recommend prioritizing research on investigating risk factors for complications in children diagnosed with SMPP and RMPP. Several studies have demonstrated that integrative treatment, which combines TCM with Western medicine, can significantly improve the prognosis of MPP, showing favorable outcomes in both SMPP and RMPP patients [ 63 , 64 ]. Future research should focus on investigating the effects of integrative treatment plans that incorporate TCM characteristics on the risk of complications in MPP. Conclusions Based on systematic reviews and meta-analyses of existing studies, the findings suggest that persistent fever, pleural effusion, radio-graphic changes, and delayed administration of macrolide antibiotics or glucocorticoids may be risk factors for complications. These complications pose a burden on hospitalized children with MPP, particularly since SMPP and RMPP patients may be at a higher risk. Although existing studies provide valuable insights, their results may not comprehensively represent the true clinical environment due to limitations related to study design, sample size, or data collection methods. Future high-quality studies are needed to validate and complement existing findings. Further research should be conducted to confirm the impact of disease stratification and treatment protocols on complication risks in MPP, thereby providing more recommendations for health policy development.
